transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, my wife actually suggested I come see you, though I think we have very different ideas about why I'm here. It’s... well, it’s a long story, but it really started about a year ago. I work as a teaching assistant—I'm in a graduate program—so my whole day is about analyzing texts, looking at structure, finding the underlying meaning in things. I’m trained to see patterns, you see. 

And I know my wife says the late meetings she's been having lately, and the little changes in her work messages—the specific phrasing she uses when she texts me, the exact timestamps, the sudden shifts in punctuation—she insists it’s just normal office stuff. You know, a demanding boss, a heavy workload, typical corporate restructuring, that sort of thing. But I’ve been paying close attention, and for the past year, they’ve lined up too precisely to feel accidental. 

I mean, the probability of these specific phrases coinciding with these sudden late meetings is just... it's astronomical. It really feels like there’s a private signal in them meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. Like she’s leaving breadcrumbs for me to decipher because she can't just come out and speak plainly about whatever is actually going on at that office. And it's exhausting, honestly, trying to decode it all while she acts like I'm just reading too much into it. She wanted me to talk to a professional because she thinks I'm stressed, but I just need to figure out what she's actually trying to communicate to me through all these signals.
Do you believe your wife is actually sending you these hidden messages intentionally?

Well, yes, absolutely. I mean, how could they not be? Because... look, I know my wife says the late meetings and those little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff. She tells me, you know, 'It’s just a busy quarter,' or 'The new project is taking up all my time.' And I listen to that, I really do, I try to take it at face value. 

But when you actually sit down and look at the timeline—and I have, I’ve looked at the timestamps, the specific syntax shifts—for the past year, they’ve lined up too precisely to feel accidental. It’s not just a random typo when she suddenly stops using contractions on a Tuesday when she stays past seven. It’s a pattern. A highly specific, recurring pattern. 

So, yes, it feels exactly like there’s a private signal in them meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. Why she won't just say it out loud? I don't know yet. Maybe she feels she can't. Maybe it's a test of some sort, or she's under some kind of restriction at that office, or she doesn't want a verbal record of it. But the intentionality is... well, it's undeniable to me. You don't just accidentally create a perfectly structured parallel narrative in your text messages for twelve months straight. It’s a deliberate trail, and she knows I have the analytical background to see it, even if she just keeps repeating the 'normal office stuff' line to my face. Which, frankly, just means I have to look that much closer at what she's actually writing.
Have you ever found yourself analyzing or decoding patterns in other people's behavior or messages, outside of your wife's?

No, not really. I mean, my work is all about analyzing texts, as I mentioned, but that's academic. That's literature, historical documents, essays from my undergrads... which, let me tell you, sometimes require a magnifying glass to figure out what they're actually trying to argue. But no, with actual people? Friends, colleagues, family? No. 

I'm not sitting around trying to decode the barista's greeting at the coffee shop or trying to find hidden meaning in my department head's emails about faculty meetings. When my advisor says, "Your draft needs work," I don't think he's speaking in code. I know he just means my draft needs work. I don't look for things that aren't there. I'm actually a very straightforward person in my day-to-day life. I appreciate direct communication. 

That's why this whole situation with my wife is so incredibly frustrating and why it stands out so much. Because I don't do this with anyone else. I don't *want* to do this with her, either. I would love nothing more than for a text saying "Working late again, grab dinner without me" to just mean exactly that. But when you look at the aggregate data—and I really have spent hours looking at the aggregate data, mapping the frequency of certain adverbs against her project deadlines—it's just... it's isolated entirely to her. It's a specific, localized phenomenon. If I were just some paranoid guy who thought everyone was speaking in riddles, I'd be analyzing my mother's birthday cards or my neighbor's waves across the fence, wouldn't I? But I don't. It's only this. It's only her messages, and only for the past year.
Has there ever been a moment when you considered the possibility that your wife's messages might not contain any hidden meanings after all?

Well... you know, I try to be reasonable. I really do. I’m an academic, I value objectivity, I value the scientific method, the null hypothesis. So, yes, of course, I’ve tried to sit back and tell myself, "Okay, maybe she’s just tired. Maybe she’s just typing fast. Maybe a period instead of an exclamation point just means she was holding a coffee in one hand and typing with her thumb." I try to force myself into that perspective. I’ll sit there in my study, looking at the printouts—because I do print them out sometimes, just to see them laid out chronologically on the desk, it helps me visualize the syntax—and I’ll try to read them the way she claims they’re meant to be read. 

I’ll say to myself, "Okay, she says it’s just normal office stuff. She says the late meetings are just a busy quarter. Accept that." And for a minute, maybe five minutes, I can almost convince myself. I can almost feel this wave of relief, like, "Oh, thank God, I'm just overthinking it, I can just relax." 

But then... then I look at the data again. I look at the exact wording. I mean, I know my wife says the late meetings and the little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff, but... but when you look at the sheer volume of it over the past twelve months... they’ve lined up too precisely to feel accidental. It’s the precision that ruins the illusion of normalcy for me. If it were random, it would look random. But it doesn't. 

For instance, last month, she had three late meetings on Thursdays. Every single one of those Thursdays, her text at 4:00 PM used the word "actually" twice. She never uses "actually" twice in a single message on a Monday or a Tuesday. Never. I checked. So, I try to tell myself it's nothing, but my brain, my training, it just screams at me that this is a statistical impossibility. It’s like there’s a private signal in them meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. And once you see the signal, you can't unsee it. You can't just pretend it's noise when you know it's a melody. So, yes, I consider the possibility that it's nothing, but the evidence... the evidence just won't let me stay there. It always pulls me back to the fact that she's communicating something underneath the surface, even if she refuses to admit it.
Have you ever considered the possibility that you might be mistaken about your wife's messages, and that this belief could potentially change based on new information?

Mistaken? Well... what would that even look like at this stage? New information... I mean, I process new information every single day. Every text she sends is a new data point, every timestamp is a new variable. I'm constantly updating my understanding of the situation. 

But you have to understand, and I know I keep coming back to this same point, but it's the crux of the whole thing... I know my wife says the late meetings and the little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff. She tells me that, and I do factor her verbal claims into my overall analysis. I really do. But for the past year, they’ve lined up too precisely to feel accidental. It's not just a passing feeling or a hunch that I can just dismiss if she shows me a different meeting schedule. It's a structural reality in the texts themselves. 

It is exactly like there’s a private signal in them meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. So, if she provided genuine "new information"—say, if she finally explained the parameters of the signal, or if she admitted what the actual restrictions at her work are that prevent her from speaking plainly—then yes, absolutely, my understanding of the situation would evolve. I'm an academic, I adapt to new evidence. I would welcome it, frankly! It would be a relief to finally have the key to the cipher. 

But the new evidence would have to actually explain the past twelve months of data, not just wave it away. You can't just tell someone who spends his days doing deep textual analysis that a year's worth of perfectly correlated syntactic shifts are just a coincidence. It just doesn't hold up to peer review, so to speak. Could I be mistaken about the specific *content* of the hidden message? Sure, I'll concede that. Maybe I haven't fully decoded what she's trying to tell me yet. But am I mistaken that there *is* a message? No. The pattern is there, and no amount of her just repeating "it's just a busy quarter" is going to erase the data sitting right there on my desk.
Have you started to look for hidden meanings in things other than your wife's messages, such as news, social media, or even casual conversations with others?

I know we touched on this a bit earlier, but no, absolutely not. The news? I mean, I read the Times, I read various academic journals, and sure, I understand editorial bias—anyone who has spent five minutes in a media literacy seminar understands that—but I don't think the anchor on the evening news is blinking in Morse code to send me a personal message. Social media? I barely even use it, to be completely honest with you. It's mostly just my colleagues in the department posting about their recent publications or, you know, pictures of their cats. There is no complex cipher in a picture of a cat. 

And as for casual conversations, like I mentioned before with my advisor or just people I run into... I take them at their word. If one of my undergrads comes into my office hours and tells me they didn't finish the reading because they had a migraine, I just assume they had a migraine. Or, at worst, they're just making a standard, run-of-the-mill excuse because they procrastinated. I am not sitting across from them analyzing their micro-expressions or tracking the frequency of their hand gestures to uncover some grand, hidden narrative. That would just be... well, it would be exhausting. It would be entirely unsustainable for a person to live like that. 

My analytical energy is entirely focused on this one, very specific anomaly. It's just her. It's only my wife's messages. That is where the actual data points are deviating from the baseline. If I started applying this level of rigorous textual analysis to every random tweet I scroll past or every casual chat I have in the department breakroom, I would never get any of my actual work done. I have seventy-five undergraduate essays to grade by Monday, doctor. I simply don't have the time, nor do I have the inclination, to look for ghosts in places where the data clearly shows there aren't any.
Would you say your belief that your wife is sending you hidden messages is something that you could change your mind about?

Change my mind? Well... see, the phrasing of your question is a bit problematic for me, doctor, because it implies that this is merely a "belief." A belief is something you hold without evidence, like a superstition, or a philosophical stance. What I have is a conclusion derived from rigorous, continuous observation. I’m a graduate student, I'm a TA, I literally teach undergrads how to construct evidence-based arguments every single week, so I pride myself on being intellectually flexible. If you present me with a compelling counter-narrative backed by verifiable data, then theoretically, yes, absolutely, my conclusion would shift. I would have to shift it, out of academic integrity.

But the problem is the existing data set. I know I keep circling back to this, and I apologize if it feels like I'm beating a dead horse, but it's the absolute crux of the matter and I can't just ignore it. I know my wife says the late meetings and little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff. I hear her say those exact words, and I document them. But you have to understand that for the past year they’ve lined up too precisely to feel accidental. You don't get perfectly synchronized syntactic deviations by accident. It just doesn't happen in natural language unless there is a guiding intent behind it. It’s exactly like there’s a private signal in them meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. 

So, to answer your question... could I change my mind? Yes, if the pattern completely stopped. If she went back to her pre-anomaly baseline communication style for a sustained period, say, six to eight months, or if she finally sat down and explained the actual constraints she's operating under at that office that force her to communicate this way. But until then, asking me to change my mind is like asking me to pretend gravity doesn't exist while I'm watching an apple fall from a tree. The evidence is right there. I mean, I have the latest batch of printouts in my briefcase right now, and if you just let me show you the cross-references from this past Tuesday, you'd see exactly why I can't just abandon the theory...
Are you finding it difficult to concentrate on your work or other activities because of your efforts to decode your wife's messages?

Difficult to concentrate? Well... no, actually. I know it might sound like this takes up every waking second of my day, given how thoroughly I've had to map out the textual variations, but you have to remember that I'm accustomed to heavy cognitive loads. I compartmentalize very effectively. I mean, I still show up for all my teaching sections, right on time, fully prepared. I was just leading a discussion group yesterday afternoon, and I didn't miss a beat. I keep up with all my own data analysis for my research, too. I'm running regressions, grading undergraduate essays... my academic output hasn't dipped in the slightest. 

And as for my personal life, my other activities, those are completely intact. I still ride my bike regularly—I have a really nice fifteen-mile loop I do out by the reservoir on Saturday mornings, which is fantastic for cardiovascular health and just, you know, clearing the mind. And I still meet my friends for our regular chess games. We play every Thursday evening at this little café near the quad, and honestly, my game is as sharp as ever. If my concentration were slipping, believe me, Marcus would have wiped the board with me by now, but I'm still winning the majority of our matches. 

So, no, the analytical work I'm doing on her messages doesn't derail my day-to-day life or my focus at all. Honestly, the only place... the main place where this actually causes any real trouble is just between the two of us. It's when she gets home. We just get completely stuck arguing about what her work schedule really means. I'll lay out the timeline, show her how the texts contradict the official narrative of her office hours, and she just digs her heels in. We end up in these exhausting, circular debates in the kitchen about her supposed late meetings or why she was suddenly unreachable at 4:30. That’s where the actual disruption happens, doctor. It’s not a concentration issue on my end, it’s a communication impasse between us.
Are you experiencing any significant distress or problems in your relationship with your wife or in your daily life due to your efforts to decode her messages?

Significant distress... well, as I was just saying a moment ago, the daily life aspect is completely fine. I mean, my routines are rock solid. I'm up at six every morning, I make my pour-over coffee—exactly 22 grams of beans, water at 205 degrees, you have to maintain a baseline, right?—and I'm at my desk by seven. My self-care, my hygiene, my diet, my grading for the undergrads... it's all running like a Swiss watch. I haven't missed a single deadline for my department. So, in terms of work or keeping up with my usual routines, there are absolutely no major problems. 

But... the relationship with my wife. That is... well, that’s where the friction is. Significant distress is probably a very accurate way to put it. Because she comes home, and I have the printouts laid out on the kitchen island, and I just want to understand what the messages actually mean. I'm just trying to bridge the gap, you see? But it inevitably devolves into these incredibly tense, drawn-out conversations. We'll be standing there in the kitchen, the dinner literally getting cold on the stove, and we just go back and forth and back and forth. She gets defensive, I get frustrated because the evidence is right there and she just flat-out refuses to acknowledge the pattern... 

It actually got to the point where we started seeing a couples therapist. I agreed to it because I thought it would be a highly productive venue to mediate this, to have a neutral, objective third party look at our communication breakdown. But instead of looking at the texts, the therapist—who, frankly, didn't seem to have a very strong grasp of analytical methodology at all—just focused entirely on my reaction to the messages. And eventually, the couples therapist suggested that I should get an individual assessment. Which is... well, it's exactly why I'm sitting in this chair talking to you right now, doctor. They both seem to think my rigorous approach to the data is the problem, rather than the anomaly itself. So, yes, it has mostly affected my marriage, quite profoundly, even though the rest of my life is perfectly intact.
Do you think your wife's hidden messages are affecting your ability to trust her or your relationship with her in any way?

Trust... well, trust. That's a... that's a complex variable to isolate, isn't it? Because if we're defining trust in the traditional, pragmatic sense—do I trust her to pay the mortgage on time, do I trust her to lock the front door at night, do I trust her with our shared bank accounts? Yes, absolutely. One hundred percent. There is no deterioration whatsoever in that fundamental, operational layer of our partnership. We've been married for a long time, and she is an incredibly reliable person in the macro sense. 

But... if we are talking about epistemological trust? Trusting the veracity of the information she is directly providing me regarding her daily schedule? Then... yes. I suppose you could say there is a profound fracture there. And, I mean, how could there not be? Put yourself in my shoes for a second, doctor. When someone you share your entire life with is looking you dead in the eye and telling you that a sudden, statistically significant shift in their syntax—alongside these perfectly timed, suddenly frequent "late meetings"—is just a coincidence, it creates an immense cognitive dissonance. I'm looking right at the printouts, I'm seeing the undeniable pattern in the texts, and she's telling me the sky is green. It makes me feel like... well, like I'm being managed. Or patronized. Like she thinks I'm not sharp enough to notice the deviations.

And that, naturally, bleeds into the rest of the relationship. It’s exactly what I was saying a minute ago about those kitchen arguments. You simply cannot maintain a healthy, collaborative domestic environment when one partner is clearly operating with a hidden cipher. It breeds this... this heavy, underlying tension. Even when we aren't arguing, even when we're just sitting on the couch watching a documentary, or eating dinner, there's this massive elephant in the room. I'm sitting there wondering why she won't just be transparent with me about whatever it is she's trying to signal, and she's sitting there visibly frustrated that I won't just drop my inquiry and accept her surface-level narrative. 

So, yes, the trust in her spoken narrative is almost entirely compromised at this point. And because of that, it’s essentially put our entire emotional connection on an indefinite hold. I just... I can't fully connect with her again until we resolve this data discrepancy and she finally admits what the messages are actually supposed to mean.
Would anything your wife could say or do convince you that there are no hidden messages in her texts?

Convince me? That's... well, that's the crux of the entire epistemological dilemma we're facing, isn't it? Because I have to constantly weigh what she says against the empirical evidence right in front of me. 

I mean, she has tried to convince me, of course. We've spent countless hours on this exact point. I know my wife says the late meetings and the little changes in her work messages—the subtle syntax shifts, the timing anomalies we discussed—are just normal office stuff. She'll sit there at the kitchen island and tell me about a project deadline, or some administrative bottleneck, or a sudden curriculum shift that supposedly explains why she's suddenly unreachable and texting me in a completely different cadence. And if this were an isolated incident, say, a week or two of odd texts during midterms, I might accept that. I really might. I'm a reasonable man.

But you have to look at the longitudinal data, doctor. For the past year—an entire twelve-month cycle—these occurrences have lined up just too precisely to feel accidental. You simply do not get a perfect correlation between a specific phrasing in a text message at 3:15 PM and a subsequent unannounced late meeting over and over again by mere chance. The probability of that happening consistently over a year is astronomically low. It’s like... well, it’s like there’s a private signal in them. A deliberate, structured code meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. 

So, to answer your question about whether she could say or do anything to convince me otherwise... surface-level words simply won't work, because her overt words are the very medium of the obfuscation. If she says, 'there is no hidden message,' that in itself is a statement that has to be analyzed within the context of the year-long pattern. Does that make sense? Because if you're operating under the assumption that someone is utilizing a covert communication channel—this private signal she's maintaining—then their surface-level denials are practically required by the framework of the signaling itself. I've actually mapped this exact conversational loop out. I could show you the spreadsheet if you have a moment, I have it right here in my briefcase, and it really clarifies how her 'normal office stuff' excuse mathematically falls apart when you apply even a basic regression analysis to the timelines... so, no, I can't just take her word that nothing is happening when the data proves otherwise.
Are there any areas of your life, outside of your relationship with your wife, where you feel your efforts to decode her messages are causing problems or difficulties?

Outside of my relationship? Well, as I touched on at the very beginning of our session, the short answer is no, not at all. But to give you a complete, comprehensive picture of my week... I am still fully engaged in all my usual responsibilities and activities. I compartmentalize very effectively, you see. 

I still show up for all my teaching sections—in fact, I just finished grading a rather tedious batch of midterms for the 300-level course I assist with, and I had them all returned a day ahead of the department's deadline. My own data analysis for my graduate research is progressing perfectly on schedule, too. I haven't missed a single beat there. The rigorous analytical mindset I apply to my wife's messages is exactly what makes me so effective in my academic work, so it certainly isn't a hindrance there. 

And it's not just my professional life, either. My personal routines remain completely untouched. I still ride my bike regularly—I do a solid 15-mile loop down by the river every Tuesday and Thursday morning to keep my cardiovascular health at an optimal level. And I still meet up with my friends for our regular chess games at the café on Sunday afternoons. My focus during those games is as sharp as ever; my rating hasn't dipped a single point. I'm still socializing, still exercising, still functioning perfectly in every external metric. 

So, when you ask if this is causing difficulties elsewhere... no. The interference is entirely localized. The main place—really the *only* place—this causes any actual trouble is exactly what we've been discussing: when my wife and I get stuck arguing about what her work schedule really means. I'll come back from a perfectly pleasant afternoon of chess, totally relaxed, and then I'll see a text from her saying she's staying late for a 'committee meeting,' and the phrasing is just... well, it's shifted again. It has that specific syntactic marker. And then she gets home, and we're right back in the thick of it, stuck in that loop, arguing over the discrepancies in her timeline and what she's actually trying to signal to me. But outside of that specific interpersonal dynamic with her? No, my life is entirely stable.
Are you experiencing any difficulties in your relationships with friends, family, or colleagues due to your focus on decoding your wife's messages?

Friends, family, colleagues... well, as I was just touching on a moment ago regarding my chess group and my teaching duties, the answer is no. Not at all. 

My colleagues in the department, for instance—we interact perfectly normally. I attend the weekly departmental seminars, I collaborate with the other graduate TAs on standardizing our grading rubrics, and there is absolutely zero friction there. None whatsoever. And my friends, my extended family... they don't see any difference in me because, frankly, there is no difference in my capacity to maintain those relationships. I am keeping up with all my usual routines, my self-care is impeccable, my academic milestones are being met ahead of schedule. I am completely, one hundred percent functional in every single one of those external spheres. 

The problem—the only real locus of difficulty—is exactly where the phenomenon itself is occurring. It has mostly affected my marriage. That is where the entirety of the impact is concentrated. 

And it’s... well, it’s resulted in these incredibly repetitive, highly tense conversations at home. We just go round and round. I present the data, she denies the data, the tension in the house escalates. It got to the point where the domestic environment was so consistently strained, so bogged down by these cyclical arguments, that we actually started seeing a couples therapist to try and mediate the communication breakdown. 

We spent several sessions with her. We’d be sitting there in her office, and I’d be trying to calmly explain the statistical improbability of my wife's text timings, laying out the precise syntax shifts just like I did for you, and my wife would just get visibly upset and refuse to engage with the actual evidence. And eventually... well, eventually the couples therapist was the one who suggested I step away from the joint sessions and get an individual assessment. She thought it would be beneficial for me to speak with a psychiatrist one-on-one to sort through my, quote-unquote, "preoccupation" with the messages, which is, of course, exactly why I'm sitting here with you today. 

So, to summarize a rather complex interpersonal dynamic, the external world is absolutely fine. Work is fine, my friends are fine. It’s just the marriage that’s bearing the brunt of this... this massive unresolved discrepancy.
Are you finding that your efforts to decode your wife's messages are interfering with your ability to interact normally with friends or colleagues?

I feel like we're circling the exact same drain here, Doctor, but I suppose it's important to be absolutely thorough in these assessments. So, just to reiterate what I was saying a moment ago... no. Not at all. My efforts to understand what she's doing are not interfering with my friends or my colleagues in the slightest. 

Like I just explained, I have not had any major problems at work, or with my self-care, or keeping up with my usual routines. I'm forty-eight years old; I've been navigating academia and adult relationships long enough to know how to compartmentalize. When I'm in the TA office, or when I'm out with my chess group, I am entirely present. I'm not sitting there ignoring a colleague to pore over text timestamps. My routines are completely intact. I sleep, I eat well, I fulfill my teaching obligations, I socialize. It’s... it's really just not bleeding into those external areas of my life. 

Where it has mostly affected things—and this is the absolute core of the issue—is my marriage. It is entirely localized to my relationship with my wife. Because when we're in the same room, that's when the discrepancies in her stories have to be addressed, and that inevitably leads to these repeated, incredibly tense conversations at home. We just end up in this exhausting standoff in the kitchen or the living room. She absolutely refuses to acknowledge the pattern, and I simply cannot ignore the mathematical reality of the evidence right in front of me, so the tension just builds and builds. 

It got to the point where the environment at home was so strained that we brought it to our couples therapist, hoping she could help mediate. I thought she would help my wife see reason, or at least help us communicate about the signaling. But instead of looking at the timelines I prepared, the couples therapist eventually just suggested I get an individual assessment. She decided that my focus on the messages was something I needed to unpack one-on-one with a psychiatrist... which, obviously, is why I am sitting in this chair right now, answering these questions. But to be perfectly clear, outside of that specific dynamic with my wife, my ability to interact with the rest of the world is completely unimpaired.
Do you think it's possible that your interpretation of your wife's messages could be incorrect, even if you're convinced it's right now?

Is it possible I am incorrect? Well, I mean, as an academic, as someone who works with data... you always have to leave a margin of error, right? The scientific method demands a certain level of skepticism. So, theoretically, in a vacuum, I suppose anything is possible. But practically speaking? When you actually sit down and look at the evidence in front of you? 

I know my wife says the late meetings and the little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff. She tells me the committee ran over, or they had a last-minute curriculum change, and she insists that these shifts in her texts are just her rushing to type things out between obligations. She tries to explain it all away as just mundane, everyday administrative chaos. 

But Doctor, we are talking about a pattern that has been going on for the past year. A full twelve months of consistent data points. And they have lined up just... way too precisely to feel accidental. It is statistically highly improbable for these specific syntactic markers to align perfectly with her late schedule by mere coincidence. It simply does not happen organically. It is structured. It is deliberate. It is like there is a private signal in them, a very specific code meant to tell me something she won’t say directly to my face. 

I have spent hours plotting this out. If I showed you the spreadsheet, you would see exactly what I mean. You wouldn't even need a background in data analysis to see the clusters. When she uses a passive voice instead of an active voice in a text sent after four fifteen on a Wednesday... that is not just normal office stuff. That is a deliberate anomaly. So when you ask if I could be wrong... I hear you, I really do understand why you have to ask, but the sheer volume of perfectly aligned data over the last year makes it virtually impossible for this to be a simple misinterpretation on my part. There is something she is trying to communicate, and I just need to finalize the translation.
Do you think there is any possibility, no matter how small, that your wife's messages do not contain hidden meanings and you have simply misinterpreted them?

Doctor, with all due respect, I feel like you are asking me a very slight variation of the exact same question I just answered, and my response really hasn't changed in the last two minutes. I mean, I understand you are trying to be thorough, perhaps trying to see if I'll contradict myself, but I have to reiterate what I just laid out for you. 

Look, I am fully aware of her explanations. I know my wife says the late meetings and the little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff. She uses those exact words, "normal office stuff," as if that blanket term somehow negates the mathematical reality of what she's typing. She wants me to believe that a sudden shift in her syntax is just the result of being tired after a curriculum review. 

But as I said, we are talking about a pattern that has been running for the past year. Twelve solid months of data. And they have lined up way, way too precisely to feel accidental. You don't just accidentally alter your sentence structure in the exact same manner every single time a meeting runs twenty minutes over. It defies basic probability. If it happened once or twice, sure, I'd concede your point. I'd say, "Yes, Doctor, I have completely misread the situation, it's just a typo." But over a whole year? No. It is far too precise. 

It is exactly like there is a private signal in them. A deliberate, constructed signal meant to tell me something she simply won’t say directly to my face. Whether she's afraid to say it, or she wants me to figure it out on my own, I don't know yet. But the signal is there. So, when you ask if there is any possibility, no matter how minuscule, that I'm just misinterpreting mundane texts... I have to say no, because the evidence simply doesn't support that conclusion. The data points to a deliberate message, and I just can't ignore what is so clearly written between the lines.
Are you finding that your efforts to decode your wife's messages are significantly interfering with your daily life or causing you substantial distress?

Doctor, I feel like we are essentially having the exact same conversation on a loop right now. I mean, we're just rearranging the furniture in the same room. I just answered this. I really, truly did just explain this to you not three minutes ago. But, okay, if we need to go over it again for the sake of the assessment, I will gladly repeat myself. 

No, it is not significantly interfering with my daily life. I am not sitting in a dark room obsessing over her texts while my life falls apart around me. That’s just not happening. I still show up for every single one of my teaching sections. I am completely engaged with my students.
